definition: What it represents is a comparison between two steady values of a quantity Q: its previous steady value, A, and its new set value, B. Their difference, B − A, is the gap the whole rest of the chain has to close — its size says how far Q has to travel, and its sign says which way: up if B > A, down if B < A. Nothing has changed yet at this step; the difference operator only measures the change that has been asked for.
name: Difference operator

definition: What it represents is two signals combined into one by adding them: the pair of the difference operator, for the places where a signal is genuinely the sum of two parts. Its place in this note is the system diagram, where a signal's position part — the value of Q at a point, constant at that point — adds with its time part, Q(t), an oscillator. Because the position part is constant, the output of the adding is an oscillator that just becomes Q(t) again: adding a constant to the oscillator does not change its kind. Adding is this operator; multiplying is the mixer, ⊗; subtracting is the difference operator.
name: Addition operator — the adder, ⊕

definition: What it represents is a signal that swings around a target value and settles onto it: it overshoots, comes back, overshoots less, and the swings die away inside a decaying envelope until only the target remains. That is the true shape of the signals in this note before they are simplified: a quantity set to a new value does not glide there — it swings around the target value B as it closes in on it. The smooth exponential is this signal with the swing removed (simplification 6), not the signal itself.
name: Oscillator signal

definition: What it represents is the spread of values across all the parts of a system at one instant — few near zero, most in the middle, a long tail of a few very large — and the single average value that spread amounts to. It stands for two steps: simplification 3, the whole set of parts and their individual values replaced by this one distribution, and simplification 4, that distribution collapsed by its integral average, ⟨E⟩ = ∫ E · P(E) dE, into the single number the rest of the chain works with. It is made before the diagram even starts and carried through the whole chain — every value anywhere in the diagrams is already this average, not any one part's value.
name: Boltzmann distribution

definition: What it represents is the signal crossing from one medium into another — a quantity passing from the medium that sets it into the medium that receives it — and coming out as the corresponding signal in the new medium: Q in the first medium becomes Q in the second. The two sides are not the same substance and do not respond the same way: the first medium is held at its value, while the second has to be brought there by contact. The medium-change math: the receiving value chases the setting value by the general law dQ/dt = k·(B − Q), so Q(t) = B + (A − B)·e^(−kt) as its mean — an oscillator in the new medium, swinging around the target, with the coupling k set by the contact between the two mediums. The kind of signal does not change across it: oscillator in, oscillator out — what changes is the medium carrying it, and with it the constants that govern it.
name: Medium change

definition: What it represents is the envelope of an oscillator signal being taken as the signal. An oscillator swings around its mean inside a decaying envelope; this converter — a type of signal converter — keeps that envelope and the mean it bounds, and drops the swing between them, so an exponential comes out where an oscillator went in. It changes the kind of signal, not its destination or its size: the exponential it produces settles to the same target, along the same mean, as the oscillator it replaces. This is simplification 6 as a step in the diagram — a conversion we perform on the signal so the rest of the chain can work with the simple form, not a process happening in the system.
name: Envelope signal converter — the envelope operator

definition:
What it represents is a signal that closes on its target at a rate proportional to the gap that remains — fast while the gap is big, slowing as the gap shrinks, levelling off as it arrives: the general settling Q(t) = B + (A − B)·e^(−kt), where A is the starting value, B is the target value, and k is the rate constant. It is the simplified form of the oscillator signal — the oscillator's envelope and mean with the swing removed — and it is the form the envelope signal converter puts out. It appears twice in the chain: once as that converter's output, and once again after the mixer, because a transform can scale an exponential's size without changing its kind — the signal at a point is still this same exponential settling, only weaker. Whether it climbs or falls is set by the signal itself, by the sign of B − A: rising and falling are the same exponential, closing the gap from opposite sides.

The equivalent diagrams. This symbol can be drawn four ways — the curve climbing or falling, toward the right or toward the left — and all four are equivalent symbols: each one stands for the same exponential signal, the same closing-on-the-target at a rate proportional to the gap. When the direction is specifically known, the drawing that matches it can be used: rising, B > A, climbs — drawn here up to the right, the form this note uses — and falling, B < A, drops. But when the direction is unknown, the four are interchangeable: any one of them can be drawn, and it still means the exponential — the direction is then carried by the signal itself, by the sign of B − A, not by which way the curve in the circle happens to lean.
name: Exponential signal

definition: What it represents is one signal scaling another by multiplication: a transform carried out as a product. In this note the mixer is where the signal meets position: the exponential Q(t) runs through a transform that depends on the point, so the value of Q at point b is its value at point a reduced by the factor the move from a to b imposes — what comes out is the same signal, reduced by exactly that factor. The mixer does not add anything of its own; it applies one input to the other. (Addition is a different operation — the adder, ⊕, defined beside the difference operator above.)
name: Mixer — ⊗

definition: What it represents is a transform converter. A transform converter is a block in a system diagram that takes a transform in one form and puts it out in another form: it changes the form of the transform — the form of the response — not the kind of signal — the underlying transform, what it does to the signal, stays exactly the same; only the form it is carried in changes. That is what separates it from the envelope signal converter (the envelope operator): an envelope signal converter changes the kind of signal (oscillator in, exponential signal out), while a transform converter changes the form a response is expressed in. A transform converter has no letter notation — it is named for the conversion it performs. This converter works on a transform that varies smoothly: in goes the transform as it actually is, a smooth curve, and out comes the same transform converted into a piecewise linear approximation — straight-line pieces standing in for the smooth curve. The transform itself is unchanged — the same effect, at the same points — only the form it is carried in changes. This symbol is not used in the main block diagram yet, but it is kept here because it can be used later.
name: Piecewise linear approximation

definition: What it represents is keeping only the settled part of a signal and discarding its transient: a filter in time, not in space. It stands for the judgement that the variable has been held constant long enough — t ≥ t_s, where t_s is the time the settling takes — that the travel from the old value to the new one can be ignored and only the arrived value kept. It is a filter because it passes part of what reaches it and holds back the rest: the steady state passes, the transient does not. This is simplification 8 as a step in the diagram, and it applies only when that condition actually holds — change the setting and the transient is real again until it settles.
name: Steady-state filter

definition: What it represents is a signal that no longer changes: one value, held. It is the end of the chain — the value of Q at a point after the transient has been filtered away, Q constant at steady state — the state the whole system was travelling toward from the moment the difference operator measured the gap. Every earlier step exists to produce this: a settled value, at a place, that stays where it is until the setting changes again.
name: Constant signal

definition: What it represents is an exponential in space rather than in time: a quantity that is constant in time at every point, but whose value falls off exponentially with distance from where it starts — a thermodynamic distance filter, the attenuation a signal undergoes as it travels through a medium. Its value at position x is set by three numbers: the initial value at x = 0, the end value it falls toward as x grows, and the cutoff rate, which sets how fast the fall happens — a large cutoff rate spends the signal quickly, a small one lets it reach far. It is the spatial twin of the exponential signal: the same closing on a value at a rate proportional to the gap that remains, but along position instead of time, so nothing in it ever changes with time.
name: Exponential transform
